articles.title: Japan's New Vending Machines Make Fresh Matcha
articles.intro: Learn about Japan’s new vending machines that prepare fresh matcha drinks, their technology, and the global rise in matcha’s popularity.

sentences.text: How strong do you like your matcha?
Well, in Japan, you'll soon be able to choose from five different strengths — all with the press of a button.
New vending machines are coming to Japan that make fresh matcha.
The machines are a little different from normal drink vending machines.
Instead of selling drinks in bottles or cans, they prepare each cup of matcha after the customer presses a button.
The idea is to give customers a drink that tastes like matcha made by hand.
The machines were made by two Japanese companies working together, Toyo Vending and Ito En.
Toyo Vending already makes vending machines that grind coffee beans and prepare each cup fresh.
Now, it's looking to bring similar technology to matcha.
Drinks company Ito En will supply the matcha powder, which is made from carefully chosen tea leaves.
Customers will be able to choose from five different strengths of matcha, as well as different drinks, including matcha lattes.
Matcha has become increasingly popular around the world.
In 2025, Japan exported 43% more green tea than the year before, partly because of growing demand for matcha.
And with more international tourists visiting Japan, Toyo and Ito En believe their machines will make it easier for visitors to try freshly prepared matcha.
The companies plan to put the machines in busy places, including train stations, airports, shopping areas, highway rest stops and areas that are popular with tourists.
The first machines are expected to appear this month, although no specific locations have been shared yet.
So for people who enjoy freshly made matcha, there'll soon be a new way to get a cup without going to a cafe!

articles.title: Tokyo Named World's Fourth Safest City to Visit
articles.intro: Explore how Tokyo was ranked among the world’s safest cities, the methodology behind the rankings, and which cities were deemed the safest for 2027.

sentences.text: Tokyo is one of the world's safest cities to visit, according to a new ranking.
Tokyo climbed up from ninth place last year to come fourth on this year's list, which ranks the world's safest cities for travelers in 2027.
Created by American travel insurance company Berkshire Hathaway Travel Protection, the ranking looked at 38 of the most popular cities with US travelers.

The company surveyed 1,500 travelers, and asked them to rank the cities for different aspects of safety, such as safety from crime and terrorism, health safety, transportation safety, and safety for women and minorities.
The survey results were then combined with safety rankings from _The Economist_ and online database Numbeo, as well as scores from travel safety site GeoSure.
Among participants in the Berkshire Hathaway survey, this year Tokyo was ranked second in the world for transportation safety — and with its famously well-run trains, that's little surprise!
The city was also third globally for safety from violent crime, and GeoSure gave it a very high score for safety at night.
However, it got lower survey scores for safety from terrorism and safety for women and minorities.
The world's safest city to visit in 2027 is Montreal, Canada.
Survey participants put Montreal first in the world for safety for women and minorities.
It was second for safety from violent crime and terrorism, second for health safety, and third for transportation safety.
After Montreal was Zurich, Switzerland.
Few survey participants had actually been there, but those who had visited gave it top scores for safety from violent crime and terrorism, and also for transportation and health safety.
Amsterdam in the Netherlands came third.
Berkshire Hathaway suggested that Amsterdam's relaxed attractions — such as walking around canals and seeing art — help to make it an especially safe place to visit.

articles.title: Paper Straws May Be Worse for Environment than Plastic
articles.intro: This lesson explores a study comparing the environmental impact of paper, plastic, biodegradable, and plant-based straws.

sentences.text: In the fight to protect the environment against waste, many businesses have swapped plastic straws for paper.

However, a report by South Korea's Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment suggests that the overall environmental impact of paper straws and their effect on human health could actually be worse than plastic.
Researchers compared four types of straws for the report — regular plastic, biodegradable plastic, paper and bio-based polyethylene, a type of alternative plastic material made from plants.
The environmental impact of each type of straw was examined, covering each one's entire life cycle from raw material production to waste disposal.
One of the main findings was that paper straws actually scored over six times higher than regular plastic straws for their carcinogenic impact.
This measures the cancer risk caused by emissions produced across an item's entire life cycle.
This does not mean that just drinking with a paper straw is a cancer risk.
Instead, it means that the ways they are manufactured and disposed of create emissions linked with the disease.

Paper straws were also found to have twice as high an acidification impact as regular plastic — this refers to how likely a product's emissions are to increase environmental acidity and harm ecosystems.
Paper straws did not have the worst results, however.
While a less common swap, bio-based polyethylene straws were found to have around 16 times the carcinogenic impact of regular plastic straws.
They also had six times the acidification impact.

Biodegradable plastic straws didn't do well either — though they were still better than paper straws, with three times the carcinogenic risk and almost twice the acidification impact of regular plastic.
The report also found that recycling straws made of any material in South Korea was almost impossible.
In reality, 74% of straws are incinerated, while 26% go to landfill.

Presenting the report, South Korean lawmaker Kim Wi-sang called on the government to move away from environmental regulations that just mean swapping one material for another, and move toward policies directly aimed at reducing single-use consumption.

articles.title: Toyota to Assemble and Sell Kei Trucks in US
articles.intro: This lesson covers Toyota's plan to assemble and sell kei trucks in the US, focusing on their features, production, and market strategy.

sentences.text: Toyota will begin assembling and selling "kei trucks" in the US next year, as higher prices for vehicles and fuel increase demand for cheaper options.
Kei trucks belong to Japan's smallest class of road vehicles, but are known for their practicality and efficiency despite their small size.
_Kei-jidosha_ vehicles — "kei cars" in English — make up about 40% of the cars driven in Japan, but have not often been sold as new vehicles abroad.
However, while American drivers typically prefer larger vehicles, rising prices for pickup trucks and increasing fuel costs have made kei trucks much more popular in the US in recent years.
According to _NHK_, more than 30,000 have been shipped to the US in the last five years.
Toyota's new "Kei-01" will be the first kei truck produced in the US.
It will be assembled in a factory in Indiana, using parts imported from Japan.
In fact, most of the parts for the new Kei-01 will come from the Hijet kei truck, which is sold in Japan by Daihatsu, a subsidiary of Toyota.
The American-made vehicles will be sold under the new brand name "Scion by Toyota."
However, the little four-wheel-drive truck will be almost exactly the same as the Japanese Hijet, and will even have the steering wheel on the right.
But Toyota believes the trucks will be popular for use on farms, ranches and small business sites, as well as for short-distance journeys.
The Kei-01 will also be modified to meet US safety rules for "low-speed vehicles," and will have its top speed limited to 40 kilometers per hour.
Toyota plans to begin selling the {{prn:Kei-01|kay zero one}}, at first just to corporate clients, in the second half of 2027.

articles.title: Fruit and Vegetable Scraps Could Boost Health — Study
articles.intro: A study finds that fruit and vegetable scraps like skins and seeds contain more fiber and health benefits than parts we typically eat.

sentences.text: Many of us throw away things like the skins, stalks and seeds of fruits and vegetables.
But we could be discarding important health benefits along with these scraps!

A study published in the _ International Journal of Food Sciences and Nutrition_ looked at 12 types of fruits and vegetables commonly eaten in the UK, including watermelon, broccoli and butternut squash.
Researchers examined the parts of each fruit or vegetable that are commonly thrown away.
They found that in 10 out of 12, there are much higher levels of dietary fiber in the parts people don't usually consume compared with those they normally eat.
For example, watermelon rinds were found to contain around 2 grams of fiber per 100 grams, which is about the same as a slice of whole wheat bread.
But the softer inside part of a watermelon has just 0.4 grams of dietary fiber per 100 grams.
Butternut squash skin and seeds offer a little over 9 grams of fiber per 100 grams — about one-third of the 30 grams the UK government recommends adults eat each day.
That's much higher than the 2 grams of fiber per 100 grams found in the part of butternut squash usually eaten.
Broccoli was the exception — the stalks that people usually throw away have 28% less fiber than the florets on top of them, which are usually eaten.
Fiber is an important part of a healthy diet, improving digestion and reducing the risk of heart disease and some cancers.
However, many people around the world don't get enough.
Using the often-discarded parts of fruit and vegetables could help — but people usually don't want to eat them.
So the researchers tried selling some recipes at foodservice outlets at King's College London.
For nine weeks, students could buy things like watermelon salad that included the rind, or an African-style peanut stew with butternut squash skin and seeds.
These ended up representing around one-third of hot meal sales during those nine weeks — and in follow-up surveys, 77% of students said they'd likely choose them again!

articles.title: 80% of People Have 'Laundry Anxiety'
articles.intro: This lesson explores a survey revealing that 80% of people feel anxious about doing laundry and discusses common laundry worries.

sentences.text: Whites in one pile, colors in another.
But wait — what temperature do these clothes need to be washed at?
Can sheets and jeans be washed together?
For some people, doing laundry is a normal part of adult life.
But according to a new survey, it makes many people anxious!
The survey was done by Samsung with 2,000 adults in the UK.
It found that 80% of people have felt anxiety while doing laundry.
About half said they're afraid to wash certain clothes because they don't want to ruin them.
In fact, only 15% feel confident washing different types of clothes!
People are most likely to avoid washing woolens, embellished clothes, coats and cashmere in the washing machine.
Others worry about how to wash vintage clothing — with 10% saying this has stopped them from buying vintage clothes altogether!
On average, each person has four items of clothing they feel anxious about washing.
Some people also said they're not sure how to wash jeans, with many saying they hand-wash them instead of using the washing machine.
So why are people so anxious?
A little over half of participants said they've ruined something in the wash.
Clothes getting smaller or losing their color were the most common problems.
Almost two-thirds said that ruining something in the wash made them more anxious about washing other clothes.
But while many have laundry anxiety, others are the opposite.
The survey found that 12% of people put most clothes in the washing machine without worrying about what will happen to them.

articles.title: Too Good to Eat: Meet the Artist Who Knits Food
articles.intro: Explore the creative world of Kate Jenkins, a UK artist who knits, crochets, and embroiders realistic, mouth-watering food art.

sentences.text: Kate Jenkins can make all sorts of dishes, from pasta to pizza to desserts.
There's just one thing — her dishes can't be eaten!
Jenkins is an artist from the UK who is known for her knitted, crocheted and embroidered creations.
When she was a child, her grandmother taught her how to knit, and she has been creating things out of yarn ever since.
In the 1990s, she worked as a knitwear designer for big fashion houses, including Ralph Lauren and Marc Jacobs, and she later started her own fashion company.
When Jenkins needed a way to promote her company, she started knitting food, both for fun and to try to get people's attention.
That became her first food-themed exhibition, called "Comfort Food," in 2007.
Her food creations were so popular that they became a very important part of her career.
Since then, she's created collections based on bakeries, cafes, ice cream shops and more.
Her newest exhibition is called "Kate's {{prn:Knitalian|knitalian}}," which is made to look like an Italian restaurant.
It opened on October 30 at the Air Contemporary Gallery in London.
The exhibition has over 100 pieces made by Jenkins, including knitted plates of ravioli, bottles of wine and even a creamy tiramisu.
Jenkins wrote on her website that everything was made to look "deliciously real."
All pieces are available to buy, and the exhibition will be open until December 5.
Jenkins also likes to add a little humor to her work.

The "restaurant" has a sign saying that it's been rated by the "Stitchelin Guide" — instead of the Michelin Guide — and another that says it's on "Knitadvisor," instead of {{prn:Tripadvisor|trip advisor}}!
"Above all, I want my work to make people smile," Jenkins said on her website.

articles.title: Concerts Are Inspiring Travel Across Asia
articles.intro: Explore how concerts, especially K-pop, are motivating international travel across Asia and changing tourism trends among music fans.

sentences.text: Some people choose their vacation destinations for the beaches, food, or famous sights.
Others choose them based on where their favorite artists are playing.
In July 2026, Trip.com Group and Live Nation Asia surveyed nearly 1,800 concertgoers across six Asian markets: mainland China, Hong Kong, Macao, Singapore, Thailand and South Korea.
According to their new report, 65% said they had traveled to another country or region for a concert.
And seven in 10 said live music was one of the most exciting reasons to travel.
But fans don't always want to go home the morning after the show — they want to see more of the place they're visiting.
On average, people said they would ideally like to spend four days at their destination.
As for where to stay, 63% said they choose five-star hotels when traveling for concerts.
And 84% were interested in packages that combine concert tickets with extras such as hotel stays, flights or visits to local attractions.
Trip.com Group said its bookings for these packages rose by 64% in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period in 2025.
Two-thirds of people also said being part of a fan community was important for them.
For Gen Z fans in particular, sharing their trips on social media was a key part of the experience.
And K-pop is giving music fans a reason to hit the road.
In Bangkok, for example, the share of concertgoers coming from other countries is nearly twice as high for K-pop shows as for other concerts.
BTS is scheduled to play three shows in Bangkok in December as part of its "Arirang" tour.
Trip.com says flight bookings to the city jumped by over 440% within three days of its ticket presale — nearly six months before the first show.

articles.title: Nvidia Investigates CEO's Affair with Alleged Chinese Spy
articles.intro: Nvidia investigates its CEO after reports of an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, exploring national security, legal, and business impacts.

sentences.text: US chipmaker Nvidia has launched an investigation into reports that its CEO, Jensen Huang, was targeted by Chinese intelligence after he admitted having an affair with a businesswoman suspected of spying for Beijing.
The company's board announced the investigation on November 8, following reports by _The New York Times_ that US intelligence officials believed the woman was gathering information for China.
In a letter to employees, Huang, 63, admitted being unfaithful to his wife and apologized to his family and colleagues.
He said he took "full responsibility" for his actions.
Nvidia's board said it had "no reason to believe" that national security or company secrets had been compromised, but that it would examine all available information.
Huang has promised to cooperate fully and will remain CEO during the investigation.
"I love our country and our company," he wrote.
"I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security."
Nvidia has become a major player in the global race to develop artificial intelligence (AI), with its advanced computer chips powering many AI systems.
These chips have also been subject to US export restrictions aimed at limiting China's access to advanced technology.
_The New York Times_ identified the woman as Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen and chip buyer.

She previously worked as a television reporter in China before becoming a top executive at Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, which bought more than {{prn:$4.8 billion|four point eight billion dollars}} worth of Nvidia chips over the past two years.
The company previously faced accusations of helping businesses sidestep US export restrictions.
However, Nvidia said its own checks found no illegal activity.
The scandal has also led to legal action.
On November 9, a shareholder sued Nvidia and Huang, accusing them of misleading investors about the affair and its possible risks to the business.
Nvidia shares fell 4.3% that day, wiping about {{prn:$190 billion|one hundred and ninety billion dollars}} off its market value.
They dropped another 5.5% on November 10.
Meanwhile, President Donald Trump said the FBI was also looking into the affair, but added that Huang had told him he had no idea the woman could be involved in espionage.
China has rejected the spying allegations, calling them unsubstantiated.

articles.title: DNA Study Tracks English Language's Ancient Origins
articles.intro: Explore the ancient origins of the English language through a new DNA study tracing early migrations and the development of Germanic languages.

sentences.text: It's reasonable to assume that English is from England — and certainly, the language we recognize today spent over {{prn:1,500|one thousand and five hundred}} years developing there.
However, English is part of a larger Germanic language family that also includes — as the name suggests — German, as well as Swedish, Danish and many other European languages.
English as we know it comes from people called the Anglo-Saxons, who traveled from mainland Europe to Great Britain in the fifth century.
Over time, their Germanic dialects developed into English.
Before the Anglo-Saxons, people across Great Britain spoke Celtic languages, some of which still exist as modern Welsh, Scottish Gaelic and Cornish.
Now a new study published in _Nature_ has used DNA to better understand how the Germanic languages spread, giving us fresh insight into the ancient origins of English.
The researchers analyzed DNA from {{prn:4,500|four thousand and five hundred}} ancient European individuals, and used that data to reconstruct how genetic groups migrated.
They compared what they found with cultural evidence like inscriptions, architecture, artifacts and burial styles to infer what languages these groups likely spoke.

This research found that the earliest Germanic-language-speaking people migrated from the Baltic region — somewhere between Finland and northeastern Sweden — into Denmark and the south of Sweden around {{prn:4,000|four thousand}} years ago.
This is actually {{prn:1,000|one thousand}} years later than experts had believed.
But within 500 years, these people's genetics were spread across Scandinavia.

The study then found that around {{prn:1,650|one thousand six hundred and fifty}} years ago, people from the south of Scandinavia began migrating down to the regions we know today as Germany, Poland and the Netherlands, again bringing their own languages.
As was the case in Great Britain in the fifth century, the languages being replaced were probably Celtic.
Migration wasn't just going one way either, and around the same time, people from what is now northern Germany also went to Denmark and Sweden.
They brought with them Old Norse, which was the language spoken centuries later by the Vikings.
They were also very genetically close to the Anglo-Saxons, which may explain later cultural similarities between the Vikings and Anglo-Saxon Britain.

articles.intro: This lesson covers a news story about an Italian chef fired in Australia for refusing to make ham-and-pineapple pizza, exploring cultural views on pizza.

Davide Tamburella was fired from La Costa restaurant in Brisbane in May this year after several disagreements with his bosses.
One was his refusal to make ham-and-pineapple pizzas for a large event.

Tamburella later took his case to the commission, saying that he had been unfairly fired.

articles.title: Why Does Japan Have So Many Commemorative Days?
articles.intro: Explore why Japan has so many commemorative days, how they're created, and the unique wordplay and traditions behind these special celebrations.

sentences.text: November 11 is Pocky Day in Japan.
People celebrate by eating and sharing Pocky, a popular stick-shaped chocolate snack.
But why November 11?
Well, November 11 can be written as 11-11, which looks like four Pocky sticks!
And Pocky isn't alone on that day.
The Japan Anniversary Association has 66 commemorative days registered for November 11, including Noodle Day and Fish Sausage Day.
Many of these days celebrate long, thin foods that look like the number 1.
So, where do all these special days come from?
Well, companies and industry groups can create them to promote their products or raise awareness of something.
The Japan Anniversary Association then registers them.
And in recent years, the association has registered more than 200 new special days each year!
Many dates are chosen using clever number wordplay.
For example, Nori-Japan, a group that promotes the health benefits of seaweed, created "Black Seaweed Day" on September 6.
In Japanese, nine and six can be read as {{prn:_ku_|koo}} and _ro._
Together, they make _kuro_, the Japanese word for "black."
For the first Black Seaweed Day, Nori-Japan gave out free seaweed sheets at Tokyo Tower, and food trucks served dishes made with seaweed.
These special days aren't only about food, though.
For example, November 26 is "Good Bath Day."
In Japanese, {{prn:1-1|one one}} can be read as {{prn:_ii_|e}}, and {{prn:2-6|two six}} can be read as _fu-ro_ — and  _{{prn:ii|e}} furo_ means "good bath"!
The Japan Anniversary Association says it has registered more than 3,000 special commemorative days since it began in 1991.
The association has also come up with some fun ideas for "commemorative years."
For example, 2028 could become "Garden Year" because the numbers 2 and 8 together can be read as _niwa_ — or "garden" in Japanese.
So if special days aren't enough, perhaps special years could be next!

articles.title: One in Four Teens Not Getting Enough Exercise
articles.intro: This lesson explores a global study showing that most teens don't exercise enough, with activity levels lower for girls and in less wealthy regions.

sentences.text: Young people across the world are not getting enough physical activity, according to a new study, with one in four adolescents saying they are not active on any day of the week.
An international team of researchers looked at around {{prn:390|three hundred and ninety}} surveys of 3.2 million adolescents aged 11 to 17 in {{prn:140|one hundred and forty}} countries.
The researchers counted an active day as one in which a person got at least 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity.
Sixty minutes is the World Health Organization's recommended daily amount of exercise for children and adolescents.
The researchers found that in 2025, almost 25% — around 240 million adolescents — reported no active days a week.
The global average was 2.7 active days a week, and just 14% of adolescents were active every day.
Across the world, girls reported fewer active days than boys, at an average of 2.4 days compared to 3 days for boys.
And while average activity for boys didn't change much as they aged, for girls there was a decline from 2.6 days at 11 years old to 2.2 days at 17.
There were also differences between regions.
In Central Asia, East Asia and the Pacific, Europe and other high-income Western countries the average was around 4 active days.
In contrast, regions where incomes are lower, such as the Middle East and North Africa, South and Southeast Asia, and Sub-Saharan Africa, averaged around 2 active days.
The study authors said regional differences could be explained by the fact that wealthier countries can afford to promote physical activity more and provide public spaces for it.
In 2018, the World Health Organization set a target for 2030 of a 15% reduction in adolescents who don't get 60 minutes of activity each day.
However, according to the study, no country or region is on track to meet that target.

articles.title: Drinking Wine Has Lower Death Risk than Beer, Spirits
articles.intro: This lesson explores a study on how different types of alcohol—wine, beer, and spirits—affect health risks and mortality rates.

sentences.text: Alcohol is linked with many health impacts, including heart disease, cancer and early death.
According to the World Health Organization, there is no safe level of alcohol consumption.
However, a study in _Nutrition Journal_ has found that beer, spirits and wine don't have the exact same health risks — with low to moderate wine consumption carrying a lower mortality risk.
The research included 340,000 participants from the UK Biobank health database.
The researchers looked at alcohol consumption rates among the participants, as well as the number and causes of deaths among them over 13 years.
High consumption of any alcoholic drink was linked with higher death rates from all causes.
The researchers defined high consumption as more than 40 grams of pure alcohol a day for men, and over 20 grams a day for women.
For reference, there are around 20 grams of pure alcohol in a 500 milliliter bottle of 5% beer.
Moderate alcohol consumption, meaning 20 to 40 grams a day for men and 10 to 20 grams for women, was also linked with higher death rates from cancer.
However, the type of alcohol people consumed seemed to matter when they were drinking less of it.
Beer and cider were linked with a higher risk of cancer death even at low-level consumption — up to 20 grams a day for men, and up to 10 grams a day for women.
Non-consumption was defined as having no more than 20 grams of alcohol a week.
At both low and moderate levels, drinking spirits was also linked with an increased risk of death by any cause.
However, low-level wine consumption was linked with a lower mortality risk from any cause, and red wine specifically was associated with a lower risk even at moderate levels.
The mortality risk increased for high wine consumption, though.
The researchers also warn that this study is only observational, and doesn't prove that wine can protect health.

articles.title: Want to Sound More Confident? Raise Your Eyebrows!
articles.intro: Learn how facial expressions like raising your eyebrows can make you sound more confident, based on new scientific research into nonverbal communication.

sentences.text: You might think that sounding confident is all about choosing the right words and speaking clearly.
But your facial expressions may matter more than you think!
A new study from the University of Glasgow suggests that something as simple as raising your eyebrows or briefly closing your eyes could make others think you're more sure of what you're saying.
The study involved 44 people: 22 native English speakers from Britain and 22 native Mandarin speakers from China.
The participants watched short videos of computer-generated faces answering "Yes" or "No" to questions such as, "Would they make a good leader?" or, "Will they finish the essay tonight?"
The researchers changed how the faces moved their eyes and eyebrows while keeping the words and tone of voice the same.
Each participant watched {{prn:1,800|one thousand and eight hundred}} videos, judging how confident the speaker appeared, from "very doubtful" to "very confident."
The results were very similar for both the English-speaking group and the Mandarin-speaking group.
Brief eye closure and raised brows made speakers seem more certain, while lowered brows and squinting had the opposite effect.
Also, the more the speaker lowered their eyebrows or squinted, the more doubtful they appeared.
However, raising the eyebrows higher did not make the speaker seem any more confident.
"When interpreting speech, listeners draw on more than just the words and voice," said Jonas Nölle, who led the study.
While previous research has shown that gestures and tone of voice affect how we interpret speech, much less is known about the role facial expressions play in showing confidence.
The researchers say their findings show that facial expressions do more than just accompany speech — they help shape how we understand what others are saying.
So the next time you want to sound convincing, remember that your face may be speaking just as loudly as your words!

articles.title: Many Americans 'Work Remotely' from the Office
articles.intro: Explore why many Americans go to the office only to work remotely, including research findings and reasons for this growing workplace trend.

sentences.text: Every morning, you wake up early, get ready in a hurry and make the long commute to the office — only to spend the next eight hours talking to colleagues through a screen.
According to a new report called _Remote Work from the Office_, this routine has become normal for many Americans.
Researchers from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York and the University of Virginia surveyed over {{prn:1,800|one thousand and eight hundred}} US workers in September this year.
On their most recent day in the office, nearly half had no in-person meetings.
Seventy-one percent were missing at least one teammate, while 15% had no casual face-to-face conversations with anyone.
And here's the interesting part: 37% joined at least one online meeting even though everyone taking part was in the same office.
"These workers commute in just to work remotely from the office," the researchers said.
So why is this happening?
One reason is that team members often work in different offices or cities, so even when employees show up, their colleagues may be far away.
Another is poor planning.
Some companies require a certain number of office days but let workers choose when to come in.
As a result, teammates often miss each other.
And some employees simply prefer video calls even when everyone is in the same office, because sharing screens can make it easier to work together.
Companies often say office time helps people share ideas, learn from one another and build relationships.
But just getting people through the office door may not be enough.

articles.title: '6-to-1' Shopping Method Could Help You Save Money
articles.intro: Learn about the "6-to-1" shopping method for saving money, meal planning, and making healthier choices at the grocery store.

sentences.text: With food prices increasing around the world, many people are looking for ways to save money when they shop.
And some people have been looking to something called the "6-to-1" shopping method.
New York chef Will Coleman first shared this system in a TikTok video in 2024, and it has since gone viral.
The idea is simple: when you go shopping, buy six vegetables, five fruits, four proteins, three carbohydrates, two sauces or spreads, and one "fun" item.
This should make at least six full meals.

Not only does this help you eat healthier food, having a structure for your shopping helps stop you from buying things impulsively — while having a plan helps make sure that you use everything you buy.
Having a system also helps you finish shopping faster.
And having little room for highly processed food and snacks means you have to think carefully about the treats you want to give yourself.
The fruits and vegetables can be fresh or frozen — and can also be used for smoothies!
For protein, you might choose chicken or beans, while rice or potatoes might be your carbohydrates.
You could get a pasta sauce or a spread like hummus, and perhaps choose some chocolate as your treat.
However, before you even go to the supermarket, Coleman says you should start by checking what you already have, and then plan out your meals for the week.
Some people who have tried his method say it has helped them take their weekly grocery bills from around $85 to about $45.
Though others say they've saved less.
So, will the 6-to-1 method make your next shopping trip cheaper?
Possibly — but even if it doesn't help you save money, it can help you make more careful choices about what you buy!

articles.title: _Godzilla Minus Zero_ Breaks Box Office Record
articles.intro: Explore how "Godzilla Minus Zero" broke box office records, its impact on foreign films, and the growing success of non-English movies.

sentences.text: Japanese monster movie _Godzilla Minus Zero_ topped the North American box office over the weekend, earning {{prn:$31.6 million|thirty one point six million dollars}} and setting a new opening record for a live-action foreign-language film.
Takashi Yamazaki's sequel to 2023's _Godzilla Minus One_ is set in Japan after World War II.
It continues one of cinema's longest-running franchises, with Godzilla recently celebrating his 72nd birthday.

The film broke the previous opening record for a live-action foreign-language movie, held by 2004's _Hero_, which earned $17.9 million, and added to the trend of international, non-English productions drawing American audiences to cinemas.
_Godzilla Minus Zero_ also earned about $17 million in Japan, where it opened at the same time as in North America.
"This historic opening shows how deeply audiences around the world connect with Godzilla and with Takashi Yamazaki's vision," said Koji Ueda, president of Toho Global, the film's producer.

The success follows that of _Godzilla Minus One_, which won an Oscar for best visual effects and became the highest-grossing Japanese live-action film in the US and Canada despite a modest budget under $15 million.
_Godzilla Minus Zero_, made for less than $20 million, is expected to surpass its predecessor's record earnings of $57.1 million.
The film has been well received by both critics and audiences, earning a 90% positive rating on Rotten Tomatoes.
Another international film, the Hindi-language epic _Ramayana: Rise of a Legend_, also had a strong opening weekend.
The first part of the two-film story, based on Indian mythology, earned $8.7 million in North America and $32 million in India.
It is the most expensive Indian film ever made.
Both _Godzilla_ and _Ramayana_ were made for IMAX, a cinema format that uses larger screens and advanced sound and picture technology.
_Godzilla Minus Zero_ earned $21.3 million worldwide from IMAX screenings, accounting for 34% of its total box-office earnings.
The film's success could either boost excitement or set a high bar for the next Hollywood, English-language Godzilla movie, _Godzilla x Kong: Supernova,_ which is due in March.

articles.title: Why Cold Showers Are Good for You and the Planet
articles.intro: This lesson explores the health and environmental benefits of cold showers, including studies on well-being, illness, water, and energy use.

sentences.text: Starting or ending the day under a frosty shower might not be everyone's favorite thing.
But it could have benefits for both your health and the environment.
Researchers from the University of Basel in Switzerland looked at over 700 people aged 18 to 65.
Some of these people took 30- to 120-second cold showers for 12 weeks.
The others — the control group — took showers as usual.
All the participants were in good health, and weren't already in the habit of taking cold showers.
They regularly reported on how their showers were going, and also reported on their health, including whether they'd taken days off work due to illness.
Not everyone was able to stick to cold showers, however.
But the researchers continued to count anyone who took cold showers at least 70% of the time as part of the cold shower group.
And it was found that the cold shower group took 31% fewer days off for illness compared to the control group.
The cold shower group also got significantly better scores on tests of their psychological well-being.
The researchers weren't just interested in the health effects of cold showers.
They also noted that people spend less time in the shower when the water is cold, which reduces their water consumption — a boon for the planet and their water bill!
Cold showers also reduce energy consumption.
The researchers estimated that each cold shower saved enough energy to power an average refrigerator for almost four hours.

While cold showers may be good for health and the environment, researcher Lena Glaser says people don't need to force themselves under icy water — because any decrease in temperature should have benefits.
"The water doesn't have to be equally cold every day," she said.
"We don't feel equally brave every day, and that's okay."
She also noted that participants seemed to gradually get used to cold showers as they continued to take them regularly.

articles.title: Change Employers for Career Progress, Workers Say
articles.intro: Explore why many workers believe changing employers is necessary for career advancement, and discuss the importance of skills and workplace growth.

sentences.text: If you wanted to move forward in your career, would you look for opportunities at your current company, or start looking elsewhere?
A new survey of more than 2,000 workers across the US and UK has found that 66% think they would need to leave their current employer to advance their career.

The survey, done by Propeller Insights for workplace assessment company SHL, found that many employees want to learn new skills and move into new roles — but do not always have opportunities to do so where they already work.
One problem may be that employers don't have a full picture of what their workers can do.
Only two in five workers said their manager understands the skills they have beyond those needed for their current job.
And 89% said they would take a skills assessment to show what they can do.
Many employees also think companies are more interested in bringing in people from outside.
Fifty-nine percent of US workers and 49% of UK workers said their employer prefers this to helping current staff move into new jobs.
Managers may also get in the way.
Nearly a third of workers said their manager not wanting to lose a good employee was one of the main things stopping them from changing roles.
At the same time, 84% said they want employers to help them find opportunities within the company that match their skills and experience.
Learning new skills is also very important for many workers.
More than 40% said the skills they would gain were more important than job title when considering a new job offer.
And more than eight in 10 said they would retrain to get a higher-level job, while a similar share would retrain to move into a different type of job.

articles.title: Greenland Opens New Airport to Attract More Tourists
articles.intro: Explore Greenland’s new airport in Ilulissat, its economic hopes for tourism, and concerns about balancing growth with environmental impact.

sentences.text: Greenland has opened a new international airport in the town of Ilulissat, hoping to bring in more tourists as the Arctic island looks to become independent from Denmark one day.
The first flight from Copenhagen, Denmark, arrived on October 29, carrying 169 passengers, including Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen.
Nielsen called the airport "one of the biggest investments" in Greenland's history.
Greenland, home to about 56,000 people, relies heavily on fishing.
Its government hopes tourism will help diversify the economy and reduce its dependence on Denmark.
Ilulissat, known as the "City of Icebergs," is one of the island's most popular places to visit.
Sitting on Greenland's western coast, more than 550 kilometers north of the capital, Nuuk, the town is home to about 5,000 people.
Visitors come to see its icebergs, take sled dog rides and go on boat trips.
Until now, travelers from other countries often had to change planes or arrive by cruise ship.
There are no roads between Ilulissat and Greenland's other big towns.
Air Greenland plans to offer up to six flights a week between Copenhagen and Ilulissat during the busiest summer months, while Icelandair will also have flights from Iceland.
Another international airport opened in Nuuk in late 2024.
United Airlines also began offering summer flights between Nuuk and Newark, New Jersey, in 2025.
But Greenland has yet to see the big increase in tourism it had hoped for.
International visitor numbers have increased by at least 65% since 2018, to almost 150,000 in 2024.
However, tourism still made up less than 5% of Greenland's economy that year.
Some people also worry about the effects of growing tourism.
Palle Jerimiassen, a former mayor in the area, said that while tourism can bring in more money, the island must be careful as visitor numbers grow.

articles.title: Sleeping in on Weekends May Be Bad for Your Heart
articles.intro: This lesson explores research linking irregular sleep schedules, like sleeping in on weekends, to a higher risk of heart problems.

sentences.text: After a busy week, staying up late on Friday and sleeping in on Saturday can feel like a well-earned reward.
But according to new research, that reward might not be so good for your heart.
A team of researchers from Harvard Medical School studied sleep data from more than 10,000 American adults who wore activity trackers for around six months.
In total, the data included over one million nights of sleep.
The researchers looked at how long people slept, when they went to bed and woke up, how much time they spent in different sleep stages, and how their sleep schedules changed from night to night.
They then followed the participants for almost four years to see whether they had heart problems.

The study — which has not yet been peer reviewed — found that people whose sleep schedules changed from night to night over the six-month period had a 20% to 23% higher risk of problems such as heart attacks, strokes and heart failure.
And every 29-minute change in how long they slept from one night to the next  — whether sleeping more or less — was linked to a 24% higher risk of these problems.
Study researcher Nguyen Minh Tuan Viet said that while people often focus on getting a full eight hours of sleep each night, keeping a regular sleep schedule is a simple way to protect heart health.
So, the next time you're tempted to stay up late on Friday night, remember that keeping to your usual bedtime might actually be a better reward for your heart.

articles.title: Special Suits Could Make Japan's Castles More Accessible
articles.intro: Explore how special suits are helping make Japan's historic castles more accessible for wheelchair users and visitors.

sentences.text: Japan has lots of castles, but getting to them isn't always easy.
Visitors sometimes have to climb hundreds of steps, and some castles aren't accessible at all to people who can't walk.
However, that may soon change!
A few years ago, a company called Techno Associates created a type of "suit" that makes it easier to walk and climb.
And last month, the city of Hikone decided to test whether these suits could help make Hikone Castle more accessible for wheelchair users.
However, the suit is really more of a set of straps worn over clothes.
It uses air pressure to provide extra support to the back and legs, reducing the effort needed to move.
They're not strong enough to help wheelchair users walk — but they can make it easier to carry them.
Hikone Castle is one of only 12 castles in Japan where the main tower is still standing.
And getting there isn't easy — there are about {{prn:140|one hundred and forty}} steps to the top.
So, on October 19, city employees and volunteers wore Techno Associates' suits to help them carry wheelchair users up to the top.
The wheelchair users sat in a wooden palanquin, which was held up by a long bar across two of the carriers' shoulders.
The suits helped the carriers support the weight as they climbed the steps.
Each team had six people, who took turns carrying the palanquin.
The carriers said the suits were very helpful on the climb, making it a lot easier to carry the palanquin.
The city is thinking of using this not only as a way to help wheelchair users visit the castle, but also as a way to let visitors experience being carried around like the nobility were in the past!
It could also be a way to make castles around Japan more accessible.

articles.title: 70% of Japanese Kids Read Less than an Hour a Week
articles.intro: This lesson explores a survey revealing that most Japanese children spend less than an hour a week reading books and how parents influence their habits.

sentences.text: Watching videos, playing games or reading books — which do you prefer?
For many children in Japan, books aren't their first choice, even if they enjoy reading.
A new survey by the Hakuhodo Foundation's Child Research Institute asked 1,200 elementary and junior high school students about their reading habits.
The survey found that just under 70% of children like reading books — however, over 70% spend less than an hour a week reading books, and some don't read at all.
In fact, about three out of four children said watching videos or playing video games is more fun than reading.
And books seem to become less popular as children get older.
Junior high school students are less interested in reading than younger children, and they also spend less time actually reading books.
However, the survey found something interesting about children who love reading — their parents often have a love of books too!
In families where parents read for at least an hour a week, more than 90% of children say they like books.

And compared with other parents, those whose children love reading are more likely to give their children books about their interests, read aloud to them, and regularly take them to libraries and bookstores.
So videos and games may be more popular with many children, but books haven't lost their place.
And parents may help keep that love of reading alive!

articles.title: 80% of Netflix Users Have Watched Korean Content
articles.intro: Explore the global rise of Korean dramas on Netflix, their international popularity, and how subtitles and dubbing boost their worldwide appeal.

sentences.text: Have you ever watched a Korean drama on Netflix?
If you have, you're certainly not alone!
According to Netflix, about 80% of its subscribers around the world have watched at least one Korean show or movie.
It's been 10 years since Netflix arrived in South Korea in 2016.
And since then, Korean entertainment has become popular in many different parts of the world.
Since 2021, Netflix has shared weekly lists of its 10 most-watched shows and movies around the world, called the "Global Top 10."
More than 210 different Korean shows and movies have appeared on these lists.
One of the biggest hits has been _Squid Game_.
The series stayed on Netflix's Global Top 10 for 32 weeks, including nine weeks at number one.
But it's not just _Squid Game_ that's getting attention from people around the world.
In Japan, _Crash Landing on You_, a 2019 story about a South Korean woman who falls in love with a North Korean soldier, stayed in the country's Top 10 for 72 weeks.
In Bolivia, the 2009 show _Boys Over Flowers_ spent 49 weeks in the Top 10, while 2021's _Vincenzo_ stayed in Pakistan's Top 10 for 45 weeks.
One reason these shows have become so popular is that they're available in different languages.
For example, the third season of _Squid Game_, released in 2025, was available with subtitles in 37 languages.
People could also watch dubbed versions of the show in 24 languages.
So 10 years after Netflix arrived in South Korea, Korean entertainment is popular in countries all over the world.

articles.title: 1 in 10 Malaysian Men Borrow Money to Pay for Dates
articles.intro: This lesson explores a survey on dating costs in Malaysia, including who pays, popular date spots, and how rising expenses impact relationships.

sentences.text: You buy flowers and you pick up your date.
Then you go for dinner and have a few drinks.
It's the perfect date — but perhaps not for your wallet!
Dating can be expensive — and a new survey has found that more than one in 10 Malaysian men have borrowed money to pay for dates.
The survey was done by LEGASI Research.
It looked at how people in Malaysia date, including how much they spend on dates, where they go and who pays.
Nearly 60% of men said they usually cover the cost of the date themselves — even with someone they're in a relationship with.
However, half of female participants said they prefer to take turns paying.
Shopping malls, restaurants and cafes were found to be the most popular places for dates.

Half of participants said they think dating has become too expensive, with a similar percentage saying they spend between about {{prn:$12.50|twelve dollars and fifty cents}} and $50 per date, mostly on food and drinks.
And 13% of men said they had borrowed money to pay for dates, compared with 5% of women.
However, more than 75% of participants — both men and women — said they would increase their spending to keep a relationship going.
The survey comes at a time when many people in Malaysia are struggling with the rising cost of living.
A different survey found that nearly one in four Malaysians aged 25 to 44 had delayed marriage or having a child — or decided not to get married or have a child at all — because of money struggles.

articles.title: Why You Should Go for a 'Color Walk'
articles.intro: Learn about "color walks," a mindfulness activity that boosts mental health by focusing on colors during a walk and noticing your surroundings.

sentences.text: It's nice to go for a walk.
You can get outside, get some exercise, and stop thinking about all the other things in your life — like work or school.
But what if you can't stop thinking about all those other things?
You might want to try a "color walk."
Color walks have been getting popular on social media.
Mental health experts say they help people slow down, look around and just enjoy being outside.
They also help you stop looking at your phone all the time!
First, choose one color and look for it on your walk.
If you choose blue, for example, you might notice a blue car or a blue flower.
When you find something in your color, take some time to really look at it.
What shape is it?
Is it big or small?
Is it all the same color, or is some of it maybe lighter or darker?
If you enjoy taking photos, you can take pictures of nice things you see in your color.
Or you can just try to see how many you can see.
This will help you think about what you're doing right now, not work or school or something you read on the internet.
You don't need to walk to a special place — it can be a place you've walked around many times before.
When you slow down and really start looking, you might be surprised by how many new things you notice!

articles.title: Tokyo Restaurant Adds Space for Content Creators
articles.intro: Explore how a Tokyo yakiniku restaurant created a special space for content creators to film, share, and enjoy meals with added privacy.

sentences.text: For some people, eating at restaurants isn't just about enjoying good food.
It's also about taking photos, making videos and sharing the experience online.
And now, a restaurant in Tokyo has designed a space especially for people who like to make every meal into a social media experience!
Yakiniku Like is a Japanese yakiniku chain, a type of restaurant where people cook meat on a grill at their table.
Usually, people enjoy yakiniku together with friends around a large grill.
But Yakiniku Like is designed for people to enjoy their own small grill, making it easy to eat alone.
However, eating alone doesn't mean you can't share your meal with others — even if they're not sitting at the table with you!
That's the idea behind Studio Like, a new space at one of Yakiniku Like's Shinjuku locations.
It's designed for people who enjoy taking photos, making videos and sharing their meals on social media.
There's a mirror with lights for checking your hair and make-up, as well as special holders for cameras that can help you film!
The space also has walls right around your table to give you more privacy, and to help keep other diners out of your photos and videos.
But there's a time limit — each visit lasts just 60 minutes, so you can't spend all day eating meat and making videos!
For people who love posting their food adventures online, Studio Like offers a new way to enjoy a meal and share it with others!
